paragraphs: Problems between workers cost Irish companies a lot of money.
A study from NUI Galway looked at conflict at work. It found that companies lose about €239 million every year. Workers do less work when they argue or feel unhappy.
People also miss work because of conflict. In private companies, workers miss about 1.42 million days a year. Workers who are bullied also feel more stress.
Working from home can make things worse. People cannot see each other's faces, so they often think the worst.
Experts say teams should agree on how to work together. They also say people should talk about problems early, before they get bigger.
Arguments and bad relationships at work cost Ireland a lot of money every year, according to research from NUI Galway.

The researchers found that conflict at work leads to lost work worth about €239 million a year. Most of this, €187.6 million, is in private companies, and almost €52 million is in the public sector. Because of conflict, workers in private companies also miss around 1.42 million days of work each year.
Another study by the same university found that workers who are bullied are much more likely to feel stressed. Bad relationships between managers and staff also cause stress, especially for women.
William Corless, who helps people solve problems at work, says working from home can make conflict worse. When people cannot see body language, they often think others mean something bad.

Experts give some simple advice. Companies should have clear systems for dealing with bullying. Teams should agree on how they work together, calm feelings before solving the problem, and speak up early.
Conflict in the workplace costs the Irish economy hundreds of millions of euro every year, research from NUI Galway suggests.

A study by John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan estimated that lost productivity caused by workplace conflict amounts to €239.3 million annually, of which €187.6 million falls on the private sector and €51.8 million on the public sector. Conflict also leads to absenteeism, with an estimated 1.42 million working days lost each year in private companies and more than 276,000 in the public sector.

Earlier research by the same team found that employees who had been bullied were considerably more likely to report frequent stress, while poor relations between management and staff were linked to higher stress levels, particularly among women.

Workplace mediator William Corless argues that remote and hybrid working can make conflict worse, because colleagues lose the body language that helps them understand each other and tend to assume negative intent.

Experts recommend formal procedures for handling bullying and harassment, agreed team principles, dealing with emotions before trying to resolve the issue, and speaking up early before problems escalate.
Friction between colleagues is far from a trivial matter: research from NUI Galway puts the annual cost of workplace conflict to the Irish economy at well over €200 million.

Researchers John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan calculated that conflict saps some €239.3 million a year in lost productivity, €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector. It also fuels absenteeism, accounting for roughly 1.42 million missed days in private firms and upwards of 276,000 in the public service.

A previous study by the same researchers found that employees on the receiving end of bullying were markedly more prone to stress, and that strained relations between management and staff took a particular toll on female workers.

Mediator William Corless contends that remote and hybrid arrangements can aggravate tensions: stripped of body language and physical presence, people are inclined to read hostility into ambiguous messages.

The remedies proposed are pragmatic: robust procedures for tackling harassment, team principles agreed in advance, soothing frayed emotions before addressing the substance of a dispute and, crucially, airing grievances before they fester.

Research conducted at NUI Galway suggests that conflict in the workplace imposes a substantial financial burden on the Irish economy, with costs estimated in the hundreds of millions of euro each year.

The study, undertaken by John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan, estimated that lost productivity attributable to workplace conflict amounts to €239.3 million annually. Of this total, €187.6 million is incurred by the private sector and €51.8 million by the public sector. Moreover, conflict contributes to absenteeism, resulting in approximately 1.42 million lost working days per year in the private sector and over 276,000 in the public sector.

An earlier study by the same researchers found that employees who had experienced bullying were considerably more likely to report persistent stress. Furthermore, poor relations between management and staff were associated with elevated stress levels, particularly among female employees.

According to workplace mediator William Corless, remote and hybrid working may exacerbate such tensions, since the absence of non-verbal cues frequently leads individuals to infer negative intentions.

Consequently, experts advocate a number of measures, including formal procedures for addressing harassment, mutually agreed team principles, attending to emotions before resolving the underlying issue, and raising concerns at an early stage.
